outlook-show-declined-meetings-on-calend.title: Keep declined meetings visible in Outlook, or get one back
outlook-show-declined-meetings-on-calend.description: Show declined meetings on your Outlook calendar in new Outlook with a work or school account, or re-accept one you declined in classic Outlook.
outlook-show-declined-meetings-on-calend.lede: Declining a meeting usually makes it vanish, which is awkward when you want to remember it exists or change your mind. New Outlook can keep declined meetings on view; classic Outlook cannot, but offers a way back. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains Microsoft’s documented options.
outlook-show-declined-meetings-on-calend.commonBelief: Once I decline a meeting it is gone unless the organiser re-sends it.

sections.heading: Who can use the setting
body: Microsoft says showing declined meetings is available only for Microsoft 365 work or school accounts. Personal Microsoft accounts (outlook.com, hotmail.com, live.com, msn.com) and IMAP or POP accounts from other providers are not supported.

sections.heading: New Outlook for Windows
body: In Calendar, on the View tab, select Calendar Settings. Go to Calendar, Events and invitations, and under Save declined events turn on Show declined events on your calendar, then Save.
Microsoft says declined events then appear on your calendar but your time shows as free. To hide them temporarily, use View, Filter, Hide declined events.

Microsoft says declined events can appear across Outlook clients, Teams and third-party calendar apps when you decline through new Outlook, Outlook for Mac, Outlook on the web, mobile Outlook or Teams. Declining through classic Outlook does not preserve the declined event across those services. The documented promise is prospective: “From now on” after the setting is enabled. Do not rely on it to reconstruct earlier declines.

sections.heading: Classic Outlook
body: Microsoft states there is no way to show a declined meeting on your calendar in classic Outlook; only accepted or tentative meetings appear. When you decline, the meeting isn’t saved to your calendar and the request moves to Deleted Items.

To change your mind, open Deleted Items (Microsoft notes you may need View, Folder Pane, Normal to see the folder list), double-click the original request and choose Accept or Tentative. If Deleted Items has been emptied, ask the organiser to send the invitation again.

sections.heading: Worked example: a declined review that comes back
body: A fictional designer on a work account declines Thursday’s design review in classic Outlook because of a clash. On Wednesday the clash is cancelled. They open Deleted Items, find the review request, and choose Accept.

Later the designer switches to new Outlook, turns on Show declined events, and declines another meeting there. It stays on the grid with their time shown as free, so they can still see what they are missing.
Check: after accepting from Deleted Items, confirm the review appears on Thursday and that its time shows as you expect.

cells: Yes: Show declined events on your calendar; time shows as free
Respond again from the event (steps not detailed on this page)
Deleted Items → original request → Accept or Tentative
Use the response options available for that account; the retention setting is not supported

practical: Confirm you have a work or school account.
In new Outlook, turn on Show declined events on your calendar.
Use Hide declined events when the grid gets busy.
In classic Outlook, accept from Deleted Items if you change your mind.
If the request is gone, ask the organiser to resend.

faq.q: Will a declined meeting block my time?
faq.a: No. Microsoft says declined events shown in new Outlook display your time as free.

faq.q: Can classic Outlook show declined meetings?
faq.a: Microsoft says there is no way to do this in classic Outlook.

sources.label: Microsoft: show a declined meeting on my calendar in Outlook

outlook-shorten-meetings-automatically.title: Make Outlook meetings end early or start late automatically
outlook-shorten-meetings-automatically.description: Turn on Outlook’s shorten-duration setting to end events early or start them late, set separate minutes for short and long events, and check existing meetings.
outlook-shorten-meetings-automatically.lede: Back-to-back meetings leave no time to move between rooms or calls. Outlook can trim the events you create by a few minutes. The setting is per account, and Microsoft doesn’t say it rewrites what is already on your calendar. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains.
outlook-shorten-meetings-automatically.commonBelief: Turning this on shortens every meeting already in my calendar, including ones other people organise.

sections.heading: Where to find it
body: New Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the web: Settings, Calendar, Events and invitations, tick Shorten duration for all events, choose the available timing option and minutes for events under one hour and for events of one hour or longer, and Save. Microsoft’s page also includes a note recommending the latest Monthly Enterprise Channel build of Outlook Desktop.
Classic Outlook: File, Options, Calendar, Calendar options, tick Shorten appointments and meetings, choose End early or Start late, set the minutes for each length, and select OK.
Microsoft lists Outlook for Microsoft 365, 2024, 2021, 2019, new Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the web for Exchange Server 2019 as covered.

sections.heading: What it affects
body: Microsoft says that once set, the setting is honoured across Outlook for Windows, Mac, the web, iOS and Android, and that it is per email account: with several accounts you set each one.

Microsoft’s page does not say whether it changes events already on your calendar, applies to meetings you are invited to, or changes what attendees see. Don’t assume it does. Check an existing meeting after turning it on, and create a test event to see the new default.

sections.heading: Worked example: building travel time
body: A fictional manager walks between two buildings and wants five minutes after short meetings and ten after longer ones. Using an account and client that offer the setting, they choose End early and set 5 minutes for events under an hour and 10 for an hour or longer. They save the setting.

They then create a 30-minute one-to-one at 14:00 and check that it ends at 14:25, and a 60-minute review from 15:00 that ends at 15:50. They also open an existing 16:00 meeting a colleague organised, to see whether it changed, rather than assuming either way.
Check: open one existing and one new event to see which changed.

cells: New Outlook / Outlook on the web
Shorten duration for all events; minutes for <1 h and ≥1 h
Shorten appointments and meetings; End early or Start late; minutes for <1 h and ≥1 h
Microsoft says the setting is honoured

practical: Pick end early or start late and the minutes for short and long events.
Set it in each email account you use.
Create a test event to confirm the new default.
Check an existing meeting rather than assuming it changed.

faq.q: Will this shorten meetings other people send me?
faq.a: Microsoft’s page does not say. Check an invited meeting after turning it on.

faq.q: I have a work and a personal account. Do I set it twice?
faq.a: Yes. Microsoft says the setting is per email account.

sources.label: Microsoft: make all your events shorter automatically

outlook-create-meeting-from-email.title: Turn an Outlook email thread into a meeting request
outlook-create-meeting-from-email.description: Create an Outlook meeting from an email: review required and optional attendees, quoted text, attachments and protected-message limitations before sending.
outlook-create-meeting-from-email.lede: When an email thread ends with “let’s meet”, Outlook can start the meeting request for you, with the thread’s people already invited. It only works for some accounts and messages. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains what Microsoft documents.
outlook-create-meeting-from-email.commonBelief: Any email in any Outlook account can be turned into a meeting.

sections.heading: Steps
body: New Outlook: select the message and, on the Home tab, select Meeting; or open the message and use Meeting on the Message tab. Enter the date, times and location, adjust attendees and send.

Classic Outlook: select the message and choose Meeting on the Home tab, or open it and choose Reply with Meeting on the Message tab. Microsoft’s other page also lists Ctrl+Alt+R, and the More (…) menu if the button isn’t visible.

sections.heading: Who gets invited and what carries over
body: Microsoft says people on the original To line become Required attendees and people on Cc become Optional. Its other page says each person in the thread is listed as an invitee by default. Review the list before sending.
Microsoft says the header and body of the original message are included in the meeting body. Its pages don’t say that the email’s attachments are carried over; add any files you need explicitly.

sections.heading: When it won’t work
body: Microsoft says Reply with Meeting is available with Business Exchange accounts. Its protected-message guidance needs a client distinction: classic Outlook’s Reply with Meeting can fail for mail encrypted with a sensitivity label or Information Rights Management (IRM). A later note directs users of protected messages to Meeting under Home > Respond in new Outlook or Outlook on the web. Do not treat the classic restriction as a universal ban across all clients. If your permitted workflow still does not work, create a new meeting using only content you are authorized to share.

sections.heading: Worked example: a supplier thread
body: A fictional buyer on a work account has a thread with a supplier (To) and a finance colleague (Cc). They select the last message, choose Meeting, and see the supplier as Required and the colleague as Optional, with the thread quoted in the body.

Before sending, they check the complete attendee list, remove internal pricing remarks from the quoted body, inspect whether the needed quote file is present and attach it if missing. They set Tuesday 10:00, verify the time and location, then send.
Check before Send: recipients, quoted thread, any files, date and time. After sending, confirm the calendar contains the intended meeting; do not rely on a post-send inspection to prevent disclosure.

comparison.heading: Email to meeting at a glance

cells: New Outlook and classic Outlook (Home → Meeting; classic also Reply with Meeting)
Not stated; attach again if needed
Classic Reply with Meeting has a restriction; Microsoft directs protected-message users to Meeting in new Outlook or Outlook on the web

practical: Select the last message in the thread.
Choose Meeting (or Reply with Meeting in classic Outlook).
Review Required and Optional attendees.
Before sending, trim the quoted text and verify any needed attachments.
Check recipients, content and scheduling details before Send; then verify the saved meeting.

faq.q: Why is the Meeting button missing?
faq.a: Microsoft says Reply with Meeting needs a Business Exchange account. In classic Outlook, check the More (…) menu and select an actual message, not a conversation header. For protected mail, Microsoft distinguishes classic Reply with Meeting from the Meeting command in new Outlook or Outlook on the web.
Microsoft says the header and body are included but does not establish attachment carryover in these instructions. Inspect the draft and attach a needed file only if it is absent.

sources.label: Microsoft: respond to an email message with a meeting request in Outlook
Microsoft: create a meeting from an email message in Outlook

outlook-events-from-email-flights-hotels.title: Flights and hotels added to Outlook from email: control what appears
outlook-events-from-email-flights-hotels.description: Control which Outlook booking-email summaries appear on the calendar, check account limits and preserve the separate privacy setting.
outlook-events-from-email-flights-hotels.lede: Outlook can extract supported bookings from email and add them to the calendar. Display choices are available by event type; the private-event checkbox is a separate setting. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains the account limits and what to check before sharing.
outlook-events-from-email-flights-hotels.commonBelief: Every booking email becomes a calendar event.

sections.heading: What gets added
body: Microsoft lists flight, hotel and rental car reservations and package deliveries from supported senders. The same page says bills, dining, event and service reservations stopped being supported from mid-August 2020, even though some older instructions lower on the page still mention them. Do not promise those discontinued types. Past events and unsupported providers are not added.

sections.heading: Which accounts
body: Microsoft’s page applies to Outlook 2024, Outlook 2021 and Outlook.com and refers to Microsoft accounts (Outlook.com or Microsoft 365). It says the feature isn’t available for Office 365 operated by 21Vianet, Office 365 Germany or government plans, and lists the regions where it is available.

sections.heading: Change it per type
body: In Outlook on the web or Outlook.com, open Settings > Calendar > Events from email. For each supported type choose Don’t show event summaries in email or on my calendar, Only show event summaries in email, or Show event summaries in email and on my calendar. Separately, the Mark events as private so only I can see them checkbox controls whether these created events are marked private; it is checked by default.

Microsoft says these settings are changed through Outlook on the web or Outlook.com, not Outlook for Windows. If the feature was turned off, turning it back on does not create events or summaries for past messages. Its classic-web notes also say package-delivery information is not added automatically for Microsoft 365 business or other commercial accounts.

sections.heading: Worked example: shared calendar, private trips
body: A fictional traveller shares their calendar with a partner and wants flights visible but hotel bookings out of the calendar. In Outlook.com they open Events from email, keep flights on Show event summaries in email and on my calendar, set hotels to Only show event summaries in email, and leave flight entries private.

Microsoft’s sharing guidance says most people you share with see the time of a private item but not its details. It also describes an exception for a delegate granted access to private events. The traveller checks the actual audience and sharing permissions with the partner rather than assuming private is an absolute secrecy guarantee.
Check: after the next booking email, confirm what the partner can see before relying on it.

cells: Don’t show event summaries in email or on my calendar
Only show event summaries in email
Show event summaries in email and on my calendar

practical: Open Calendar settings → Events from email in Outlook.com or Outlook on the web.
Choose a display option for each reservation type.
Keep entries private unless others need details.
Confirm what calendar viewers see with a real booking.

faq.q: Why doesn’t my restaurant booking appear?
faq.a: Microsoft says dining reservations were discontinued in mid-August 2020.

faq.q: Can my shared-calendar viewers see flight details?
faq.a: These events are private by default. Microsoft says most shared viewers see only their times, but delegates granted access to private events are an exception. Check your actual sharing permissions before relying on this.

sources.label: Microsoft: automatically add events from your email to your calendar

outlook-recover-deleted-calendar-items.title: Recover a deleted Outlook calendar event: Deleted Items first, then the server
outlook-recover-deleted-calendar-items.description: Restore a deleted Outlook appointment or meeting from Deleted Items, then from the server’s recoverable items, in new and classic Outlook.
outlook-recover-deleted-calendar-items.lede: A deleted Outlook appointment usually goes to Deleted Items first, and can sometimes be recovered from the server after that. The steps differ between new and classic Outlook. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains what Microsoft documents.
outlook-recover-deleted-calendar-items.commonBelief: Once Deleted Items is emptied, a calendar event is gone for good.

sections.heading: Step 1: Deleted Items
body: New Outlook: switch to Mail, select Deleted Items, select the event and choose Restore on the Home tab. Microsoft says the item is restored to your calendar.
Classic Outlook: select Deleted Items (or Trash), select the calendar item, then Home, Move, Other folder, choose Calendar and OK.

sections.heading: Step 2: recover from the server
body: If it isn’t in Deleted Items, Microsoft directs you to recover deleted items from the server. New Outlook: select Deleted Items, then Recover items deleted from this folder at the top of the list, tick the item and choose Restore. Classic Outlook: select Deleted Items, then Home, Recover Deleted Items from Server, select the items, choose Restore Selected Items and OK.

For new Outlook, Microsoft explicitly says recovered calendar items go to Calendar. For classic Outlook, the short server-recovery page does not specify the destination for each item type: inspect Calendar and Deleted Items after recovery, and use the Calendar-item move procedure above if it is in Deleted Items. These short pages do not establish a universal retention window or account eligibility. If the server option is missing or the item is absent, ask your administrator or consult your account’s current recovery guidance.

sections.heading: Meetings are different from appointments
body: Restoring a record is not evidence that everyone’s meeting response or cancellation state has been reversed. The recovery pages do not document automatic re-invitation. If you cancelled a meeting you organized, confirm the current arrangement with attendees before sending anything else; agree whether a fresh invitation is needed and make clear which record to use.

sections.heading: Worked example: a personal appointment and a team meeting
body: A fictional user on a work account deletes a personal appointment by mistake and empties Deleted Items. In new Outlook they open Deleted Items, choose Recover items deleted from this folder, find the appointment, tick it and Restore. It reappears on the calendar.

The same day they had cancelled a team meeting they organized. After recovering their copy, they contact attendees to confirm the cancellation had been received and agree whether a fresh invitation is needed. If they send one, they clearly identify it as the replacement and avoid leaving two apparently active meeting records.
Check: open the restored items on the calendar and confirm date, time and attendees.

cells: Deleted Items → Move → Other folder → Calendar
Recover items deleted from this folder → Restore
Recover Deleted Items from Server → Restore Selected Items

practical: Look in Deleted Items first.
If emptied, use the server recovery option for your client.
Confirm the restored item on your calendar.
For a meeting you cancelled, confirm the arrangement with attendees before deciding whether to send a replacement.
Ask your administrator if recovery options are missing.

faq.q: How long can I recover deleted calendar items?
faq.a: The Microsoft pages used here don’t state a time limit. Ask your administrator.

faq.q: Does restoring a cancelled meeting re-invite attendees?
faq.a: These recovery pages do not establish automatic re-invitation. Confirm the current arrangement with attendees and send a replacement only if needed.

sources.label: Microsoft: recover deleted items from the server

outlook-calendar-color-categories.title: Colour-code your Outlook calendar with categories
outlook-calendar-color-categories.description: Use Outlook colour categories to tag calendar items in new Outlook, classic Outlook or the web. Categories are personal: attendees don’t see yours.
outlook-calendar-color-categories.lede: Categories let you colour individual Outlook items by project, client or type, independently of which calendar they’re on. They are your labels, not the organiser’s. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains.
outlook-calendar-color-categories.commonBelief: If I colour a meeting red, everyone in the meeting sees it red.

sections.heading: Assign a category
body: New Outlook and Outlook on the web: right-click the event and choose Categorize, or open it and choose Categorize on the Event tab, then pick a category. Repeat to add more than one. Use Manage categories or All Categories for more options.
Classic Outlook: right-click the item and point to Categorize, or use Categorize in the Tags group of an open item. All Categories lets you create new ones.

sections.heading: Categories are personal
body: Microsoft says a category applied to a meeting you received does not affect the other person’s Outlook view; the selection applies to the item in your own calendar. The same category list can be used for other Outlook item types such as mail, contacts and tasks. This is a personal organization tool, not a sharing or access-control setting.
Categories also differ from calendar colours, which colour a whole calendar. Use calendar colours to tell accounts apart and categories to tag individual items.

sections.heading: Worked example: a consultant with three clients
body: A fictional consultant creates three categories, Client A (blue), Client B (green) and Admin (grey), and applies them to meetings in their work calendar. A meeting with both clients gets two categories.
When Client A’s project manager sends an invitation, the consultant tags it blue on their own calendar; the project manager’s calendar is unaffected.

Check: in week view, inspect the items tagged for each client before agreeing more work. For a meeting with two categories, count its duration only once if calculating total occupied time; do not assume an item’s displayed color represents every assigned category.

cells: A category you apply to a received meeting does not change the sender’s Outlook view

practical: Create a small set of categories for your main projects or types.
Apply them with Categorize; add more than one where needed.
Use calendar colours to separate accounts, categories to tag items.
Don’t rely on categories to signal anything to attendees.

faq.a: Microsoft says a category you apply to a received meeting does not affect the other person’s Outlook view. Use explicit communication, not a personal category, to signal something to attendees.

faq.q: Can one meeting have two categories?
faq.a: Yes. Microsoft says you can assign more than one.

sources.label: Microsoft: assign a color category to a calendar event in Outlook
